utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before you commence, Mr. Waespi, I'll take this opportunity to give a decision on a Prosecution motion that was filed on the 2nd of May, requesting that the statement of witness W-146 that had been previously admitted with redactions and pursuant to Rule 92 bis be admitted pursuant to Rule 92 quater on the grounds that the witness proved to be unable to complete the 92 bis requirements owing to her medical condition. The Defence did not respond to this motion. The Chamber has reviewed the material provided by the Prosecutor and notes that the statement was given before an investigator of the Prosecution with the assistance of a certified interpreter who read the statement back to the witness. The statement is cumulative and, in addition, the medical documentation attached to the motion shows that the witness is suffering from the consequences and complications of a stroke. The Chamber is satisfied that the witness is unavailable and finds from the circumstances in which the statement was made and recorded that it is reliable. As such, the Chamber admitted the statement of witness W-146 redacted as specified previously pursuant to Rule 92 quater. Mr. Waespi, you may now proceed with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Veljovic.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Morning, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to speak into the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, please speak in the microphone. Perhaps you should come closer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I have a number of questions for you this morning, and I'd like to tell that you if you don't understand any question, please get back to me and ask me to clarify. Is that okay?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now what's your profession currently?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you please repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm a technician for the final process of lumber processing, timber processing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So you are back to the job you had before the war started? I think you told us you were a wood cutter.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, what was the last rank you had in the military?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Veljovic. Now, let's talk a little bit about what you testified about your specific role in the brigade in 1991 or 1992. Just tell us again, what was the name or number of the brigade you were part of in 1992, just before the JNA left. What was the name or number of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the withdrawal of the Yugoslav People's Army into the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the name of my brigade was the 216th Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you said that the deputy commander was Asim Dzambasovic?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And who was the commander?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Milosevic, Dragomir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And after the withdrawal of the JNA, was there a renaming, a renumbering of that brigade; and if so, into what denomination?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was no change of name. It was the Army of Republika Srpska that was established, and it changed the name of the corps and the corps determined the names of the brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And did that brigade at one time become the 1st Romanija Brigade?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was called the 1st Brigade within the Sarajevo-Romanija Brigade; whereas, the 216th was its name in the 4th Corps of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And so the SRK, the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, as it was called when it was a VRS corps, was previously the 4th Corps of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Only similar buildings were used, or rather, the same buildings, but different officers came on orders from the Ministry and the Supreme Command for commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I accept that. But just the name changed from the 4th Corps of the JNA into the SRK of the VRS; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that, because I was not involved in politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you said that Dragomir Milosevic was the commander of the 216th Brigade. Do you know for how long he had been the commander of the 216th JNA Brigade?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember, I remember that Dragomir Milosevic was commander of the brigade from the summer of 1989.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Summer 1989; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's when I met him. Maybe he came earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And in May 1992, what was his rank, the rank of now General Dragomir Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The rank he had was that of colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, did at that time Colonel Milosevic remain the commander of the 216th Brigade once it was transformed into the Romanija Brigade?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So who became the commander of the brigade you were a part of?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 216th Mountain Brigade, 99.99 per cent of its complement were reserve soldiers and officers from the territory of Sarajevo, Sokolac, Vlasenica, Han Pijesak, and Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Veljovic, the question was: "Who became the commander of the brigade that you were a part of?" Do you know who became the commander of that brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It did not have any soldiers. There were some active duty officers. There was partially withdrawal on the 19th, and I don't know if anybody was there, because it became an invalid brigade in the territory of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Let me follow up. What was your function in, let's say, August 1992 within the army?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was an operations officer in the 1st Romanija Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the 1st Romanija Infantry Brigade was part of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps in August 1992?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And who was the brigade commander of the 1st Romanija Infantry Brigade in August 1992?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander was Colonel Dragomir Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Now, do you know how long Colonel Dragomir Milosevic stayed the commander of the 1st Romanija Brigade, as far as you can tell?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Commander Milosevic remained commander of the 1st Romanija Infantry Brigade from May, the 19th of May, 1992, until the month of February 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And your role, you told us that you were an operations officer. How long did you stay in the 1st Romanija Infantry Brigade as an operations officer?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was an operation officers within this brigade from the 19th of May, 1992 until the 19th of December, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness. Let me go back to something you said, I think it was yesterday when you described the area of responsibility of the 1st Romanija Brigade and you told us --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And if I could ask that map ter number 02829 be retrieved.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You told us, Witness, that the brigade was grouped, starting from south, Grbavica, against the clock, towards east, up north, to Spicasta Stijena. Do you remember saying that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us who was your neighbouring brigade in Grbavica? Who was west of your brigade?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: West, our neighbour on the left, if you look at the north of the map, was the 1st Sarajevo Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, I just want to focus on Grbavica. Do you see Grbavica on the map in front of you?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you told us, as I just explained, that your brigade spread from Grbavica to the right, and I'm asking you which was the brigade which was spreading from Grbavica to the left? And perhaps the usher can help you later to make a marking. But please just answer the question, if you can. Which was the brigade that was left of your brigade?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The left neighbour was the 1st Motorised Sarajevo Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And can you make a marking, in fact a strike, which marks the separation line between your brigade and the 1st Motorised Sarajevo Brigade in or around Sarajevo, please.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you make a marking which would indicate that on the right side, it is your brigade; on the left side, it's the 1st Motorised Sarajevo Brigade. Maybe a little bit longer marking, if you can do that.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is it. Djukica Potok. That's a brook.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Very well. Can you please add the letter A, please.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here? Here? The letter A, where I marked it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just below that blue line, a large letter A so we can follow the transcript later.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now, to the north in Spicasta Stijena, you said that's where your area of responsibility ended. Which was the brigade that followed, again to the left, from Spicasta Stijena, the SRK brigade?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992, up until the month of September, it was the Kosovo brigade; and after that, the 3rd Sarajevo Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So in 1994 and 1995, left to your second marking was the 3rd Sarajevo Infantry Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Its name was Kosevska, the Kosovo brigade, during the first six months of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And in 1994 and 1995, it was called the 3rd Sarajevo Infantry Brigade?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sarajevo Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you please add the letter B on top of this second marking?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness. Now, can you tell us where was the headquarters of your brigade, of the 1st Romanija Brigade?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We often changed the command post. It was here in the village of Miljevici up until October 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you please attach a letter C next to your headquarters so people read the transcript can later identify and follow your testimony.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Thanks. It is a small C, but I think we can see it. Where was the headquarters of your brigade in 1994 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the region of the municipality of Pale to the west of the Derventa crossroads, about 800 metres to the west, at a motel called Alpina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But I take it in 1994 and 1995 you still had kind of an observation post, or perhaps even a forward command post, at this location here, which you had -- have identified as C?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1994, in the month of September, the 1st Romanija Brigade was not in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So what was the brigade that covered the area of responsibility of the 1st Romanija Brigade, as outlined by you right now?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The battalions in Grbavica: The Trebevic Battalion came to belong to the 1st Motorised Brigade, the Kresevo Battalion belonged to the 3rd Sarajevo Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understood your answer. Which SRK formations, which formations of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps were located around the demarcation line between Grbavica, spreading to the east, up to Spicasta Stijena from 1994 onwards? Which brigade or which battalions?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The battalion that covered Grbavica and the battalion that covered Trebevic by the decision of the commander were attached to the 1st Sarajevo Motorised Brigade. The Kresevo Battalion from here to here was attached to the 3rd Sarajevo Infantry Brigade. The same people remained there and the same commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And who was the commander who remained there?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the 1st Sarajevo Motorised Brigade was Colonel Veljko Stojanovic; whereas, the commander of the 3rd Brigade was Colonel Dragan Josipovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And where was the headquarters of the 1st Sarajevo Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Over here, somewhere in Lukavica. I don't know exactly, but somewhere here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And where was the headquarters of the --

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partly over here in the barracks; that is to say, that it changed due to activities. There always had to be alternatives, so it's roughly these two locations, but sometimes I just happened to be there, but just sometimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You just marked two different spots about two centimetres apart from each other in the area of Lukavica, for the benefit of the transcript. Can you tell me, where was the headquarters of the 3rd Brigade you have mentioned a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Somewhere around here, in Vogosca or behind Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And was there still a headquarter at the location where the 1st Romanija Brigade had its previous headquarter? That's the location you had marked as C.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me move to an exhibit you discussed yesterday with the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Before that's being done, could this map be -- become an exhibit, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P740, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If the exhibit, Defence Exhibit 185 could be retrieved, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, Witness, yesterday you remember that you were asked questions about the Judges about the "Osa" weapon, which was mentioned in a report you have signed in September 1992; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just have a look. I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And while this is being retrieved, I don't think that's the right exhibit. It's Defence Exhibit 185, which is a document dated 13 September 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me quote what you said yesterday, Mr. Veljovic. You said, "The Osa is," and I quote you, "a firing at the Jewish Cemetery held by the Romanija forces. Osa was an anti-rocket launcher intended to destroy bunkers and other armoured vehicles." That's at page 20 of yesterday's transcript. Do you remember having said that, Witness?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's not an anti-rocket launcher. It's a rocket launcher intended for destruction of armoured vehicles, bunkers, fortified positions and, at the same time, it also destroys personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. Now, when you said yesterday that it was "a firing at the Jewish cemetery held by the Romanija forces," which Romanija forces were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Parts were at the Jewish cemetery, which means that our forces didn't hold it completely. They held only one part facing Grbavica were held by our forces, the 1st Romanija Brigade, to be precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Of the SRK?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, looking at this document again. In paragraph 2 it says, and you testified about that yesterday, "that units of the brigade respond only in exceptional circumstances when enemy fire reaches such intensity that endangers lives of our soldiers." That's something you wrote; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What is the basis of your knowledge? How did you know at the time that you were drafting that, that units of the brigade responded only in exceptional circumstances?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each unit, a company, a platoon, a squad, a battalion, sent to the operations centre of the brigade, there are daily reports; and on the basis of those reports coming from battalions and brigade -- the battalion and brigade drafted their reports and sent them to the corps command. We had radio communication and wire communications at the operations centres, and immediately the battalion commanders reported any provocation to the centre about what was happening on the separation line between the two armies, or rather, what kind of combat activity was in progress.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And it was the duty of the subordinate units to portray an accurate picture of what was happening in their area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So you, being the operations officer, were aware, were completely aware, of what was happening in the area of responsibility of your brigade?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, provided I was in the brigade at the time, if I was not elsewhere on a leave. But there was a duty operation officer who collected information on a daily basis, and it need not have necessarily be me. I could have been perhaps 20 kilometres away with another battalion or other unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And all that information that comes in and is collected in the operations centre is analysed on behalf of the commander of the brigade, so he can make his decisions about how to proceed?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The commander of the brigade receives a report, and the duty operations officer and the operations and training organ prepare their regular combat reports to be sent to a higher command. These reports had to be approved by the brigade commander. In his absence, that would be the Chief of Staff. In his absence, though, this will have to be approved by an operations officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you also orally brief the Chief of Staff or the brigade commander about what was happening in your area of responsibility or is it only done by written reports?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both orally and in writing. Written reports were sent to higher ranking units, and the commander of the brigade received oral reports from the operations officer about the events involving the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me move to paragraph 4 of this same document. You have briefly touched on it yesterday. It talks about the killing of a civilian in the Soping area and that the case was reported to the military police which has been investigating it. Do you remember what was the outcome of the investigation by the military police?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Who would know about the outcome of this incident?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The intelligence and security organ and the commander. But there were killings every day; and, normally, if it didn't have during combat operations on the front line, then the military police would investigate whether someone killed that person from the inside; that is, by our forces. They wanted to establish the exact circumstances of the killing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the victim was a civilian?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness. If we move on to the next subject, and this is your role as an operations officer under the accused, Dragomir Milosevic. Now, you told us last week and also yesterday, today again, I believe, that in December 1994, in fact on the 12th of December, 1994, you became the operations officer or an operations officer of the SRK?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 12th of December, I received an order from the 1st Romanija Infantry Brigade to be transferred to the 1st Corps, and I arrived at the corps command on the 19th of December, 1994, so that would be a week later or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I'm interested now in your specific duties as an operations officer. What was your job?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A corps operations officer's duty is to prepare combat documents, maps, and to communicate with all chiefs and services to pile -- compile all orders to be on duty and is occasionally engaged in the focus of combat operations, together either with at commander or the Chief of Staff. At times, he could be assigned a command duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And who was your immediate boss, who was your superior?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My first immediate superior was Colonel Cedomir Sladoje.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And he was the Chief of Staff of the SRK?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And how many people worked alongside you? Were you the only operations officer under Colonel Sladoje or were there other operations officers?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a lieutenant with me; and in my operations and training department, there should have been a chief of that department. We didn't have one, and it also should have between 10 and 11 operations officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Where was your office?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lukavica, the command post, the barracks, the Princip Seljo barracks. The forward command post were at Trnovo, Nisici, or Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you visit the forward command post as well?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Would you sometimes accompany the -- General Milosevic to these forward command posts?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: We'll come to that later, but let me continue about your -- your prime office at Lukavica. Was it the same building that Colonel Sladoje had his office in?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And was it the same building Dragomir Milosevic had his office in.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Was it on the same floor as the office of Colonel Sladoje?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: On which floor were you located?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The operations centre was on the ground floor. The commander was on the floor, he was on one side and the Chief of Staff on the other side, and they used it at the same time as sleeping quarters. And most of the time when I was at the command post, I spent time in the operations centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me just clarify. You said your office, the operations centre was on the ground floor. That's correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please repeat that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You said that your operations centre, your office was on the ground floor?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Only I had a small room where I slept, so I was able to stay there, but I had to be most of the time at the operations centre, provided I was not elsewhere on the mission visiting the units and surveying the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the office of Commander Milosevic was where? Was it on the first floor? Was it on the second floor?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the first floor, and the operations centre was on the ground floor, but there were other offices, too, there. It was the same building where the command post was housed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you told us on Thursday about that map, how it came into existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And this is, Mr. President, Your Honours, D59, the big map, which is besides the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, when did you see the map for the first time after the war again?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was demobilised in 1996, on the 24th of February, and I became commander of the 4th Sarajevo Brigade on the 7th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: My question was: When did you first saw the map again after the war? Did you see it in 2002? Did you see it when you came to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only after my arrival in The Hague, I saw it with Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Where was that map located during the war? Was it in your office in the operations centre?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This map was in the operations centre, and another map was with the corps commander in his office. It was protected with a curtain so that if somebody from a higher instance came to visit, he was able to discuss certain situations and use the map in the process.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Was that map up to date?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And who kept it up to date, the map which was hidden behind the curtain in General Milosevic's office? Was that your job as well?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But he himself could have made some entries on the map in his position as a commander, and the same applied from someone from a -- higher ranking levels. It was his right to do so, and he also could have ordered a new map to be drawn if it was smeared or it didn't correspond to the standards of a proper working map.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I don't know whether you know, but if you know, can you tell us what was the basis of the information General Milosevic had to alter the map, if he in fact did so. Were that visits to subordinate units?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He could make changes in the map as he pleased, but I don't think that he did so. He usually asked operations officers to do that, and we were not supposed to know certain things. It was important that he knew what we were doing, and we did not need to know everything that the commander was doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You told us on Thursday that you had personally received an order from the Chief of Staff, which, as we know, is Colonel Sladoje, to draft documents about the defence in 1995. Do you remember testifying that?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Since in 1994, we had to shift as a result of the BH army action and the true picture during the truce and the issues of defence had to be reflected in the map, so that we knew the exact deployment of personnel and equipment on both sides. And as an operation officer, I immediately started drafting these documents following an order, and that was a usual practice in every army, including the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you have received the order to do these things, you have outlined by your superior. That is Colonel Sladoje?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And that's the way staff works, that people do what they are told by their superiors; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And, in fact, that's the way an army works as a whole, that people are ordered to do things and they have to report back after they have done things.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A map is reviewed, corrected, altered, amended, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You told us, I believe it was yesterday, that you were "familiar with almost everything that happened at the corps level." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not about everything, but I was pretty familiar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And that would even more apply to the Chief of Staff, which is Colonel Sladoje?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is very probably that he was more familiar; and as you go up to a higher level, the knowledge expands. There were meetings between the commander, deputies, Chief of Staff, assistant for information, assistant for morale and legal affairs, and the assistant commander for logistics as a corps meetings. The Chief of Staff conveyed orders to specific branches such as infantry, engineering units, artillery, anti-aircraft artillery units, the chief of communications, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So what was the role of the Chief of Staff? What was his function as you were able to observe while you were one of his subordinates?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Chief of Staff was, at the same time, a corps deputy commander. In the absence of the commander, he was at the head of the Corps Staff, apart from the assistants that I just mentioned. When acting as a deputy, he was in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So it's probably fair to say that he was the alter ego of the commander. They were very close to each other. Because if the commander was away, was absent, if somebody happened to him, he has to be able to take over at any time?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And the two of them always coordinated the actions and how the command and control was going to be performed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Was part of your duties as an operations officer also to take notes when subordinate commanders, brigade commanders would visit the corps commander?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but not always.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: How many times would the commander - and I'm talking about Dragomir Milosevic - call meetings that involved all subordinate commanders, commanders of brigades, of independent battalions, and so on?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it didn't happen often. It most probably happened once in a month or twice in a two month or in a fortnight, depending on the situation. Sometimes it happened that there is were two meetings in the course of ten days.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: When you needed information as part of your job to maintain these documents, to maintain the map, you were able to get information from subordinate units. You could request information from subordinate units. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What kind of information would you request from subordinate units? Can you give us examples?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I communicated with the brigade operations officer inquiring whether they had carried out certain orders, conducted training, and everything that concerned the operations and training organ. I talked to the operations officer -- officers, and I didn't issue orders to brigade commanders nor was I able to do so, unless I had a specific approval by either the commander or the Chief of Staff, if I wasn't assigned to do the inspection and checking up. But I was not authorised to issue orders to brigade command unless I was given approval in specific instances.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Was there a subject you could not get information about from the subordinate units? Were there some secret dealings you were not supposed to know about?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were supposed to know things, but many things are not revealed, just like in any structure or organisation, and by their token in an army, too. That is why security and intelligence organs exist, the ones involved in intelligence and those involved in counter-intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And who was the assistant commander of security and intelligence in your corps in 1994 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The consistent commander for intelligence and security was Colonel Marko Luganja.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And he was reporting to the Chief of Staff or directly to the commander?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He reported directly to the commander, and they also had a special channel to the Main Staff. This security and intelligence organ is usually quite an independent one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So I take it you say they had a professional communications line to the chief of security of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Most likely because I was not involved in any security issues, I dealt with the combat-related issues and training .

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So you don't know about these issues?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very little, except if we were to draft some orders for defence, then the intelligence organ was supposed to give me some information about the grouping of forces so that I could plot that on to the map. But as to how they gained intelligence, what they did in the intelligence and security organ, that was not something that I knew about.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So you didn't know about the sources, but you received information from them which you could use for your work.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, only as far as combat-related issues were concerned, in order for us to be able to direct our units as properly as possible so that they can perform their tasks properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And an example of that information would be, I take it, positions of the enemy, strength of the enemy, weaponry of the enemy; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, is it correct that sometime in August 1995 you became a brigade commander yourself?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And that was the 4th Sarajevo Light Infantry Brigade, near Pale?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you remember when you were appointed or when you actually took effective command of that brigade?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took effective command of the brigade on the 7th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I think it was a fairly well-staffed brigade. I think about 89, 90 per cent of the men you were supposed to have you actually had?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when the battalions were shifted from some other brigades, they were attached to me. That was the Jahorina Brigade from the 1st Romanija Brigade, the Trebevic battalion from the 1st Sarajevo Motorised Brigade, and the -- another battalion from Gorazde area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So that is about correct, you had almost full strength in your brigade?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I didn't have enough support artillery and I had to rely on the corps artillery, and I was appointed the acting commander because the operations officer was supposed to take part in figuring out the establishment of the brigade, the logistics, all other forms of support. And that is how I was appointed the acting commander of this brigade, and I remained in this post until after the Dayton agreement was signed; and then I remained there for two months, two additional months, and then I ended my military career.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You briefly talked about your assets available. I think you had a few tanks and also relied occasionally on sniper ammunition; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were very far away from the city, and we couldn't use snipers to target the city at all; and if we had any snipers, we probably did have, they could only be deployed on our positions to target enemy soldiers and we were not within the range of the city. Our snipers were not within the range of the city, and I can state that with full responsibility and we can check that on site, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I wasn't asking about Sarajevo. I just asked whether you had tanks and sniping ammunition, sniping weaponry available to your brigade. That's the only issue I wanted to ask you.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a tank. I had a sniper using 7.9 ammunition, but not more than four or five such snipers in the whole brigade. I had one tank, one APC, and that's all. I didn't really have any other armour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness, for these answers. Let's move on to another topic. You talked yesterday a little bit about the dealings you had with General Dragomir Milosevic. And, in fact, in the notice you got from the Defence about what you're going to testify, it said that you were one of the closest associates of Dragomir Milosevic. Is that correct, were you one of the closest associates of Dragomir Milosevic during the time he was commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not one of his closer associates, but he did have some respect for me as an officer, my character, my conduct, my honesty, and my general attitude towards the service.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So you never told the Defence that you were one of his closest associates?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but I was close.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And how close were you? Were you a personal friend of his, or was it a purely professional relationship you had, based on respect?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a professional relationship because in combat operations, the operations officer must accompany the commander to coordinate combat operations and to propose certain positions to be taken; and then the commander is, of course, free to accept or not accept the suggestion, but the commander must not be alone on the focus area of the combat operations. There has to be somebody from the staff; and because we weren't that many, I often accompanied him during combat operations. I was close to him in those situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And he -- you knew him very well also because you were already an operations officer in his brigade in 1992, when he was commander of the 1st Romanija Brigade. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I would not have joined the corps had he not held my work in high regard and also my character.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you were even made a brigade commander, an acting brigade commander, after that, which is quite a career for a staff officer.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the operations officer in the corps was at the same level as the brigade commander, but somebody from the operations organ must always be there to help with the establishment of a brigade. We didn't have enough high-ranking officers, and that is why I was appointed to this post until a proper -- properly educated and trained colonel could be find to tack up this post. One who had undergone all the proper training and education and had proper schooling and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you just told us that you often accompanied General Milosevic during combat operations, and I believe also yesterday you said that General Milosevic was often in the field. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. That would be a real soldier, always on the front line, highly respected by the officers and soldiers alike, precisely because he was always there where the fighting was at its worst. He was not always just sitting in his office or where the civilians were.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But how was it possible for him to keep abreast of what was going on if he was always sort of out where things were happening?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as in every army, we had communications equipment, we had our corps tables, and we were always able to find out what is happening. If you say "four, four, four," that means that at such and such a spot we had casualties or combat operations began. We would put in those codes, and we would immediately know what is happening. We knew that the enemy was monitoring our communications, unless, of course, we used the land lines, then we were able to talk freely. Everybody has the same system, every army: Belgians, Serbs, Muslim, German, you name it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So I take it from what you're saying that General Milosevic had a very good sense of what was going on at the front lines of his corps?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He knew about those things, but not about every minor detail. It was impossible. You had all kinds of people serving in the army, people with criminal background, people who had been taken out of the prison, convicts. Because of the situation, this is how it was. You would have doctors, professors, engineers. In particular, in the prison, in a war situation, people would be let out of prisons, convicts, so you would end up having murderers in your ranks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: How does that relate to -- to the notion of General Milosevic knowing what was going on had his area of responsibility, these criminals?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand that question. Well, let us see whether he can answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there were people who had served their sentences, and they were assigned to various tasks during the war. Some had come directly from prison and so on. And when you have a war, they're mobilised. Those convicts are mobilised and they are assigned to their units, just as people who have Ph.D.s.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I understand you now. Did these people pose a problem for you?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sometimes yes, but then the military police would intervene. And sometimes those really bad criminals did some really bad things, but then the security organ took care of that because they had lists of those people, and they really kept tabs on these people to prevent them from stealing military secrets or committing crimes or doing things that were not in compliance with the orders, against the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And always these dealings with the military police, with these people, these really bad criminals, was General Milosevic aware of those or was that something you give as an example he couldn't be aware of because it was one of the minor issues he wasn't aware of?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in any army, there are minor details that you don't really know, but they were always closely monitored, lest they should do something, but you had all kinds of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But the situation was under control with the help of the military police, is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, 95 per cent, I'm sure of that. But it's impossible to achieve 100 per cent control over everything, and that's how it is everywhere, in every army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just a couple of points, a little bit more into details about movements of General Milosevic, if you're aware of them. How often would you see him? Would you see him on a daily basis, even several times during a given day?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sometimes I would see him several times a day and sometimes we would spend days at the position, and sometimes five or seven days would pass without me seeing him at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you mentioned a moment ago that you accompanied him to subordinate units. Did you visit front lines with him?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you give us examples of the front lines you visited when you were with him?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there's hardly a location or a trench on this map that we had not really visited as we toured the positions, and we actually went to every trench on this long front line, not once, but several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You and General Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Milosevic and I, sometimes I would go alone depending on the task we were given. Sometimes one would go to one side, one to the other, one would accompany the general, and sometimes communications officers would say also tour the front line. And because everybody had to inspect their own branch, then the operations officer would get all the information and put everything on the paper and the Chief of Staff would then be given all this information, check whether it is all accurate, and that would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So if you visited front lines on your own, you would report back orally or in writing so that ultimately the commander would be informed about what you have seen visiting the front lines.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Sometimes we would report to the Chief of Staff, and the Chief of Staff would then report to the commander as the highest member of the staff; and then sometimes in the morning or in the afternoon, we would have briefings. The commander would be there, and everybody would report on the activities of the day before, what was observed, what shortcomings, and then everything would be taken care of, branch by branch.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And who would be present during these briefings?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the whole staff was present at the briefing, all the assistants and all the chiefs, together with the Chief of Staff were present there. And sometimes you would have a briefing for the staff with the brigade commanders and their assistants for security, intelligence, and so on. That was not the usual practice, but it sometimes happened that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, do you know whether at one time General Milosevic was wounded and had to go under treatment?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were together. A tank from the opposite side hit our trench. I had lost consciousness, but I was not injured. I already had some experience because my trench had been hit twice already by a tank shell, so I knew what to do. I opened my mouth, and I was not injured; whereas, other people got injured. You could have various abdominal injuries, internal injuries, ear injuries, and this is what happened in the command bunker where quite a few officers were present. Quite a few of them got injured, and one soldier, who was with us, he was quite seriously injured, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You just described the incident when General Milosevic was injured. That was in the command bunker when other people were injured as well?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Where was that command bunker located?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was at Trebevic, above Zlatiste at an elevation there, and they had a line of vision from Zuc from the opposite side. It was about two to three kilometres away, and a tank shell had our command trench.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If we could retrieve, again, 02829, please, the map, that would be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: When did that incident occur, when the command bunker was hit by a tank?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on the 17th of May, 1995, above -- just above Zlatiste.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And do you know when General Milosevic went to treatment?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he underwent treatment in August, because there was some complications following his injury.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you know where he went to go for treatment?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably, he underwent treatment at the Military Medical Academy in Belgrade, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you know when he left for treatment and how long he stayed away for?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date because on the 7th of August, I took up my post as the brigade commander, and I did not go to the corps every day, so I can't really remember the exact date. But I do know that he returned sometime in September.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And who replaced you as the operations officer of the corps when you became a brigade commander in the beginning of August 1995?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sladojevic was appointed the chief of operations organ. He was a colonel. I can't recall his first name, but he was appointed to that post. Sladojevic, something like that; he was a colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Was he a competent officer?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Highly educated, highly competent officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And do you know whether the relationship you had with General Milosevic, the professional relationship, continued while Colonel Sladojevic was the operations officer of the SRK?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if it was Sladojevic or maybe something else. I can't really remember. But I think their relationship was quite correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And who was in charge of the corps when Dragomir Milosevic went for treatment in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His deputy, Colonel Cedomir Sladoje.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you said that Dragomir Milosevic came back from Belgrade sometime in September, I believe?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember, but I think that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you know if he came back earlier than he expected?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that, and I was not in a position to know that. In fact, I was not supposed to know that, because I was not supposed to ask the commander at all. I only addressed him when I needed to. There was the chain of command, and the superior officer issues orders. The subordinate is supposed to comply with those orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I don't know whether you know the answer to that; but when Dragomir Milosevic came back to the corps area sometime in September, do you expect that the deputy commander, the acting commander, Sladoje, fully briefed General Milosevic upon his report about the events that occurred during his absence?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not present, so I don't know if he briefed him fully, but I am convinced that it was so because it was his duty to fully brief him. But I can't tell you that, because I was not present there anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So you're saying it would be the duty of the acting commander to fully inform the old and new commander when he came back from his absence?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And before the break, if we could briefly have a look at the map we have discussed already. It's probably not on the map, but approximately, can you point to the location of the command bunker when it was hit by a tank in May 1995?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, while we're waiting for the picture, it seems to me that you keep talking about a command bunker and the witness keep talking about a trench, at least in the translation that I receive. So maybe you could clarify if it is an a concrete bunker or just a trench.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Judge Harhoff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you tell us, Witness, what facility was hit? Can you describe the facility that was hit by that tank in May 1995?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A bunker is just a better fortified trench. There was no concrete. There was just a wooden, some thick wooden planks to cover it, then some rocks, then some thick planks on top, and then again some rocks. Because had the bunker been hit directly, we would all had died. But the shell hit this cover and it hit an area that was 830 centimetres above our heads. And had it not been for this cover, we would all had been killed by the force of detonation itself and yet no shrapnel penetrated this area. It is a very heavy shell, 100-millimetre calibre, 20 kilograms in weight. This was here in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Can you mark it with a letter A, but please a large letter

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a dot you have put where you say that --

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: That's great. Thank you very much for that. How far away from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Judge Mindua has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Mr. Waespi, but I have a question. Witness, please, regarding your military career, you said that you became brigade commander when you were a major. Generally a brigade commander is a general, you know, or a colonel, maybe a lieutenant-colonel in the extreme cases, but you were just major. And you said that as major, you were in charge of corps operations because there were not enough high-ranking officers. But I note that when you were appointed brigade commander, Colonel Sladojevic becomes operations officer. So where did he come from, this Colonel Sladojevic? Was he a member of the corps along with you, at the same time as you? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel Sladojevic hails from Banja Luka. That's where he was born. And where he was before he came to us, I don't know. But I know that he used to be brigade commander in Subotica, during peacetime. Afterwards, what he did afterwards, is something that I don't know, except when he came to our corps as operations chief. I was not operations chief, chief of the operations department. I was the highest ranking operations officer after the chief, because the chief of operations is the deputy of the Chief of Staff and stands in for him when he is absent. Now, why I was appointed to the such duties with this kind of rank, the law provides for that possibility in a case of war. And we Serbs say when there are no young girls, make do with an old lady as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine, fine. You've answered my second question, in part, the second question I wanted to ask you. Because when you needed a colonel, there was one in Banja Luka that was obtained. But you as major you became -- you became brigade commander after the operations. So I'm wondering whether it is maybe because you had an excellent relationship with General Milosevic. You said you had a good personality and so on. Because military-wise, you were an engineer in the lumber trade to start with, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A technician, a technician, not an engineer, but I completed the reserve officers school for the infantry. I was appointed brigade commander because there weren't enough personnel, and it wasn't a final appointment. It was a temporary appointment both times until the commander came in, because officers are sent to help set up a brigade staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, on that note, we'll take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I wonder whether Judge Mindua's question has been sufficiently answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Could we please return to that map here. How far away from the Pale-Lukavica road was that "bunker" you marked as -- with the letter A?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right above the road. If you were there above Zlatiste, you know where it is. Vertically, there is this big rock and that is where it was, so that we'd have a better view.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And as the crow flies, the distance in metres between the road and the bunker?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a rock that is right above the road. So it's just higher up, but it's right there. It's just a few metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Veljovic. What was the bunker's purpose? Was it a forward command post? Was it an observation post?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know that on the 15th, 16th of May, combat activities started at Debelo Brdo and here towards Zlatiste, and that is why since we were in danger because the enemy forces could have cut off our communications and made it impossible for to us receive resources that were indispensable for the population and the army. That is why most of us from the command where the thrust of the combat activities was, although we were, the corps command, we were there on the very front line in order to boost the morale of the troops and also in order to make the right decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And for how long, if you recall, had General Milosevic been at that position above the Lukavica-Pale road before the bunker was hit by a tank?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were there an hour or an hour and a half before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And that was on -- on which day? Was it on the 15th or the 16th of May?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was on the 17th of May, sometime in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, he decidedly said on the 17th of May. He did not mention the 15th or the 16th at all. The first time he was asked, he said it was on the 17th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. That clarifies it. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And on the 15th and 16th of May, were you and/or General Milosevic also at that location, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As soon as combat started, we came to that location. Here from the Lukavica command, we came there straight away.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness speak notice microphone all the time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, please speak into the microphone. The interpreter is not hearing you very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We, from the command, from the corps command, from the command post of Lukavica, we came there to the separation line to one of the command bunkers. It was that bunker there that had been built in the Galic days.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And just to make things clear, when did combat start in those days?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, in this area of Debelo Brdo, it was from the 13th, 14th, 15th, 16th, 17th, 18th, and so on, up to the 20-something. The fighting went on for about seven days.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If this map could be exhibited, please, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P741, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Witness, I would be interested to know just to have an impression of the level of military intelligence that both parties exercised on the other. Was it your impression that the ABiH intelligence knew about General Milosevic's presence in that bunker the day he was hit and so whether that was an attempt to take him out, or was it just a random firing against one of the military targets that the ABiH had identified?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Most probably, the intelligence service knew that General Milosevic was there in the bunker, because General Milosevic was always on the front line in all fighting. And they knew that that was the best target of all, the command post, the command bunker, the general, and they probably got their best people to guide fire from the tank in order to destroy it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And following up or following on Judge Harhoff's question, likewise, the intelligence you had of the enemy positions in the city was also very good?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm smiling because I had suggested to Judge Harhoff that he ask the very same question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we knew, too. We had quite a bit of information about the deployment of their forces, but some particular bits of information were totally inaccessible. So there wasn't 100 per cent intelligence and that is impossible, otherwise it would be very ease to resolve a situation in their favour or in ours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But you certainly knew where the ABiH positions were, where the headquarters were, at all levels where the communications were. That was privy to you?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we did not know exactly, but things changed during the course of a particular day or a week, and sometimes the wrong kind of information would arrive as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you know who Mirko -- Marko Luganja is?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have already said that Marko Luganja was Commander Milosevic's assistant commander for intelligence and security.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. He in fact told the OTP, confirmed what you just said, that it was extremely good the information the SRK had of the ABiH positions. And he told us, and I can quote, that: "Their positions, their assignments were familiar to us. We knew where their command posts were at all levels, communications centre, roads that are used for transport and evacuation. The way they reinforce their units, and all these activities took part mostly in the urban part of the city; that is, in the city itself." That is what the chief of the intelligence of the SRK told us. Would that be consistent with the way you saw things?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, most of it, yes. But that he knew everything, 100 per cent, that would not be true. But most of it, yes. There is no one who knows everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I agree. Let's move on to another topic. You told us this morning, when I asked you about the sniping capabilities of your brigade, the one you took over after August or in August 1995, and I quote you, you said on page 24 this morning: "We were very far away from the city, and we couldn't use snipers to target the city at all." You remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So I take it if you were closer to the city, you were able -- you would have been able to target the city with snipers.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would be able to, but we would never do that kind of thing to the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: We will get to that in a moment, but let me ask you on the issue of looking into the city. You told us on Thursday that "the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps couldn't really look down into the city, that the only area which was kind of dominant was Trebevic and Trebevic was a forested area." That's on page 45 and 47. Is that your testimony? That the only dominant feature the SRK had around Sarajevo was at Trebevic Mountain and that was a forested area, so one cannot open fire precisely from there?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, that we dominated at Trebevic; and from Trebevic, we could not see the city, except from the place where the funicular would get out from town. That was used by citizens for recreation purposes, and also the Muslims could not see our villages, only the woods and a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But, of course, I take it that the observation post where the Corps Staff was located in to observe the battle in May 1995 was a good viewpoint over the city.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was only a good view of town from Zlatiste, the so-called number 8. After that, in Trebevic, there is just wood and you cannot see anything all the way to Pale, except for where the funicular arrives?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So what could you see from that bunkers that was hit by the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We could observe Debelo Brdo well, and it was at 3 to 400 metres away. Also we could see the deployment of their trenches that were squid-shaped, and we could see the part of town that is on this other side of the Miljacka river, or rather, on the right bank of the Miljacka, that part of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Okay. Fine. So you could see parts of the city from your observation point. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Most of the city on the right bank: Zuc, Grdonj, Sedrenik, Kosovo, and the parts that are there when you cross the river, right over here from this place where the bunker was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So if you had weapons --

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The left bank of the Miljacka, we could not see, because underneath Debelo Brdo there are these rock that are simply cut off and then and you cannot see.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness speak into the microphone all the time. He tends to moves away from the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're being asked again, Mr. Veljovic, to speak into the microphone all the time. That may require you to move further, move your chair closer, or to lean forward. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So, if Witness, if you had - I'm not saying you had - but if you had weapons, direct weapons located at that observation point, could you have hit, not only seen but also hit, the areas you just outlined a moment ago. Just a hypothetical question for you.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. Weapons do not have that kind of range, but in order to have a tank up there -- even if a tank were there, it would be destroyed by the enemy because this would be a target. And only a bigger weapon with bigger calibres could be used. This is two kilometres or two and a half kilometres away, and there are no infantry weapons that have that kind of range and, therefore, it could not succeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Very well. Incidentally, you don't need to see the city, you don't need to see the target if you use indirect weaponry, such as artillery, mortars, air bombs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mortars, artillery, yes. Air bombs, this is an imperfect weapon, I don't think so. And we know that mortars can fire directly and indirectly, and that is known all over the world. In all armies of the world, people know about that, and all military institutions that deal with that, academies and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But you need to have an observer who sees the target, even if you fire with artillery and mortar, so they can guide the fire into the target and make corrections.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That is the basic rule, that there are artillery observers, but there are also sometimes situations in a war that no one can see parts of the terrain at certain points in time and then the targeting is approximate, in accordance with a map. Fire is guided by plashets and by maps as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Would you fire into an urban environment without having proper observation just using, as you call it, approximate targeting?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Urban targets were prohibited by an order, and we were not supposed to violate such orders without the corps command with -- vis-a-vis built-up areas. We were allowed to open artillery fire only at separation lines where the soldiers of the enemy side were. That is what was underlined. What could happen was that a projectile might simply miss a target because the targeting was not done properly, but that would be 50 metres or 100 metres off target; or if there was not a sufficient charge, or if the gun powder charge got damp, or if there were other technical deficiencies, that kind of thing can happen. If artillery is firing from the other side, and they're helping us, then it might happen that if the charge is damp, that the shell does not have a proper range and then it falls into a built-up inhabited area of town. But we were careful about that kind of thing, and sometimes a soldier would be upset, psychologically, and would forget to measure the right angle and would not do things properly and a mistake could be made. But to intentionally target something like that, no. And also from the urban area when they were targeting our positions, they could have the same kind of shortcomings, too. And often this did happen because their manufactured weapons were of lesser quality; and if they targeted Zuc, then due to technical deficiency, their shells would fall on their own units or the urban part. And that happens in all armies in the world, and the French army in the First World War had over 10.000 casualties from their own army. They were targeting at such close range that often the shells would fall on their own troops, and I would often hear this kind of communication and they would say, Friendly fire killed three of our own soldiers, and things like that. So it's that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me ask a couple of follow-up questions. Do you know of one single incident of friendly fire of the ABiH of the 1st Corps firing out of city, if it happened, according to you, that the target, accidental target would be inside the confrontation line. Can you give us an example?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These things happen often on both sides. So many times our shell hit our trenches. Due to short range, we sustained casualties. Ten, 20, 50 soldiers lost their lives; and on their side, this number was even higher, I suppose. As you saw yesterday, the deployment of support forces was such that they could hit a building due to the trajectory. Maybe the circumference of the shell does not fit the barrel, and the ceiling of the shell was such that exhaust gases were -- exhausted. So there was no mistake-free firing. Sometimes the shells fell 20 metres short of a target, and that happened to us on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And if an incident like that occurred, and if there were casualties among soldiers or civilians, that would surely make its way into a combat report off that day, at battalion level, brigade level, or corps level. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. When a mortar barrel burst on our side, it was reported, and other similar incidents. That's what happened in the 1st Romanija Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
